hints: When you reach a node with a child layer, you must finish that whole child layer before continuing on the current layer. Which traversal order does that remind you of?

Depth-first traversal: output a node, then (recursively) its child layer, then continue with next. An explicit stack avoids deep recursion: push next first, then child, so the child is processed first.

1. If n == 0 return an empty list.
  2. Push node 0 on a stack.
  3. Pop a node, add its value to the result.
  4. If it has a next, push next; then if it has a child, push child (child pops first).
  5. Repeat until the stack is empty; return the result.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.idea: Visit node, recurse into the child layer, then move to next. Same idea; depth can reach n.

approaches.name: Optimal: explicit stack
approaches.idea: Preorder traversal with a stack: push next, then child.

explain: Sample: layer 1 is 1→2→3, node 2 has child layer 4→5, and node 5 has child 6. We pop 1 (push 2), pop 2 (push 3, then child 4), pop 4 (push 5), pop 5 (no next, push child 6), pop 6, then finally pop 3. Output: [1,2,4,5,6,3]. Pushing next before child is the key detail, because the stack is last-in, first-out.
recognize: A list where nodes can open a nested sub-list that must be expanded in place → depth-first (preorder) traversal.
javascript: function flatten(vals, next, child) { const out = []; const go = (c) => { while (c !== -1) { out.push(vals[c]); if (child[c] !== -1) go(child[c]); c = next[c]; } }; if (vals.length) go(0); return out; }
